grade.first_issue: The claim that the nondecreasing sequence L_{min,n} must stabilize because otherwise it would eventually exceed a_n is unjustified: both sequences may grow indefinitely, and nothing proved forces L_{min,n} to overtake a_n.
grade.summary: The submission gives a useful covering-modulus characterization of the greedy step and a valid conditional finite-state periodicity argument. However, it never proves the crucial finiteness/stabilization needed for that reduction, and its later attempt to extend eventual periodicity to all indices contains further invalid inferences. The theorem is therefore not established.
strengths: Correctly expresses a_{n+1} as the least next multiple among covering moduli.
Correctly observes that L_{min,n} is nondecreasing.

If a fixed finite family of covering moduli were available, the argument that the increment function is periodic modulo their common multiple and hence yields eventual translation-periodicity is essentially sound.

errors.description: Unbounded growth of L_{min,n} does not imply that it eventually exceeds the independently growing sequence a_n. This unsupported assertion replaces the central finiteness argument.

Even assuming L_{min,n} stabilizes, it is false that every member of L_n must eventually be formed using only a subset of Q*. Coverings may select prime divisors outside Q* from later terms, so the claimed fixed finite family L is not obtained.

The assertion L_{n+T}⊆L_n is false; only every element of L_{n+T} is divisible by some element of L_n. Although that particular step might be repaired using such a divisor, the written inference is invalid.

From d_n≤d_{n+T}≤d_{n+2T}≤⋯ and eventual equality of successive tail values, one obtains only that the chain eventually becomes constant, not that its eventual value equals d_n. Thus the final backward extension from eventual periodicity to all n is unsupported.
